intro: Utah's biggest London plane stands in Liberty Park, 505 centimetres round and 30.5 metres tall. Five state champion trees from Utah's big tree register make up this page. Two stand together on one corner of Washington Square, a hackberry and an Ohio buckeye about 15 metres apart. Two more grow on Temple Square: a European wych elm beside the Tabernacle, and a Cedar of Lebanon at the temple that, by the story told of it, arrived around 1949 in a suitcase. None has a recorded planting date, and if you know one, tell us.
meta_description: Utah's champion London plane, 505 cm round, stands in Liberty Park. Five state record trees in Salt Lake City, from Washington Square to Temple Square.
question_meta: Nobody has dated Salt Lake City's champion trees. The biggest is Utah's champion London plane in Liberty Park, 505 cm round. Where to find all six.
question_answer: No planting date is recorded for any of the six trees we map in Salt Lake City, so the oldest is not known. The biggest is the state champion London plane in Liberty Park, 505 centimetres round and 30.5 metres tall. The best documented is the Cedar of Lebanon on Temple Square, which the Deseret News reported arrived around 1949 as a seedling seven inches high.
question_context:
All six come from the big tree register of the Utah Division of Forestry, Fire and State Lands, which measures trunk, height and crown and records no planting dates. Each one is the largest of its species in the state.

Four stand downtown. The champion hackberry and the champion Ohio buckeye share the southwest corner of Washington Square, around the City and County Building. The wych elm stands at the northeast corner of the Tabernacle on Temple Square, and the Cedar of Lebanon at the southeast corner of the Salt Lake Temple, a few minutes' walk apart. The London plane is in Liberty Park, about three kilometres south-east of downtown. All six are free to visit.

Temple Square has been under renovation since 2020, with work expected to finish by the end of 2026, and parts of the grounds have been closed during it. The cedar was measured in 2019, before the excavation around the temple began, so it deserves a fresh look from anyone passing.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Salt Lake City?
faq.a: Nobody knows. Utah's big tree register, the source for every tree on this page, measures size and records no ages. The one tree with a documented arrival is the Cedar of Lebanon on Temple Square, reported to have come to the square around 1949 as a seedling seven inches tall. If you know the history of any of the others, tell us.

faq.q: What is the biggest tree in Salt Lake City?
faq.a: Of the trees we map, the state champion London plane in Liberty Park: 505 centimetres round, 30.5 metres tall, with a crown about 26 metres across, measured in 2025. It stands north of the park's tennis courts.

faq.q: Can you see the trees on Temple Square during the renovation?
faq.a: Partly. The whole west side of the square, where the Tabernacle and its wych elm stand, has been open to visitors since February 2025. The cedar stands at the southeast corner of the temple, where work continues until the end of 2026, and we have no dated sighting of it since 2019. If you go, tell us what you could see.

trees.name: The Liberty Park London Planetree

location.address: Liberty Park, north of the tennis courts, Salt Lake City

trees.access: Free, in the public city park Liberty Park, open daily
trees.transport: Liberty Park, about 3 km south-east of downtown; walk from the park's 700 East or 900 South edges
trees.story:
The biggest London plane in Utah stands north of the tennis courts in Liberty Park, and it is five metres round. The Utah Division of Forestry, Fire and State Lands lists it as the state champion of its species and as a Heritage Tree, and its foresters measured it in 2025: a trunk 505 centimetres in circumference, a height of 30.5 metres, and a crown spreading about 26 metres, not far short of its own height.

The park around it has a well-recorded history. The land belonged to Brigham Young from 1860, he is recorded planting trees on it, and Salt Lake City bought it from his estate in 1881. On 17 June 1882 the 80-acre parcel opened as Liberty Park. It is tempting to give the tree those dates, and nothing supports doing so: no source we have found says when this plane went in, or ties it to Young's planting or to the park's opening. It could be a nineteenth-century tree or a twentieth-century one that simply grew fast.

What the record does give is the measurement, and it was taken last year, so the tree was standing then. London planes are the hybrid that lines streets from London to New York, with bark that flakes off in patches of grey, cream and olive, and this one is the largest of its kind that Utah has on its register.

Nobody has dated it. If you know when it was planted, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size: a London plane 505 centimetres round and 30.5 metres tall, with a crown about 26 metres across. It stands in Liberty Park, north of the tennis courts.

trees.name: The Washington Square Hackberry

location.address: Washington Square, 451 S State St, Salt Lake City (southwest corner)

trees.access: Free; the public grounds around the City and County Building, open daily
trees.transport: Downtown; a few minutes' walk from the Library or Courthouse TRAX stops
trees.story:
Utah's champion hackberry is wider than it is tall. The state's Division of Forestry, Fire and State Lands measured it in 2018 at 18.3 metres high, with a crown spreading 24.7 metres and a trunk 373 centimetres round, and the register lists it as a Heritage Tree as well as the biggest of its species in the state. A hackberry is a tree of the American interior, with warty grey bark and small berries the birds strip in autumn. This one grew into the shape of a shade tree.

It stands at the southwest corner of Washington Square, the block that holds the Salt Lake City and County Building. That building had a turbulent start: its cornerstone was laid in July 1892, it was finished in 1894 after stoppages and a financial panic, and it was designed to rival the Salt Lake Temple as the city's architectural centrepiece. When Utah became a state in 1896 it served as the first state capitol, until the present Capitol opened in 1915. How much of that the hackberry was here for, nobody has written down.

The square is public ground and free. An observation logged at this spot in May 2025 shows a tree standing there, which is the newest sign of life we have. Its neighbour about 15 metres away is the state's champion Ohio buckeye, narrower and slightly taller.

Nobody has recorded its age. If you know when it was planted, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, about 25 metres across on a trunk 373 centimetres round. It stands at the southwest corner of Washington Square, about 15 metres from the narrower, taller Ohio buckeye.

official_register.name: Big Trees register for Salt Lake City (ArcGIS Big_Trees layer, state champion records), no. OBJECTID 150

trees.name: The Washington Square Ohio Buckeye

location.address: Washington Square, 451 S State St, Salt Lake City (southwest corner)

trees.access: Free; the public grounds around the City and County Building, open daily
trees.transport: Downtown; a few minutes' walk from the Library or Courthouse TRAX stops
trees.story:
The taller of the two state champions on this corner of Washington Square is the slim one. Utah's register measured this Ohio buckeye in 2018 at 19.2 metres, almost a metre above the champion hackberry standing about 15 metres away, on a trunk of 213 centimetres and a crown only 13.7 metres across. Two record trees of two different species, on one corner of a city block.

The Ohio buckeye is a Midwestern tree, Ohio's state tree, and a long way from home on the Wasatch Front. Buckeyes are among the first trees to leaf out in spring, opening hand-shaped leaves of five leaflets, then pale yellow-green flower spikes. In autumn it drops spiny husks holding a glossy brown nut with a pale eye, the buckeye that gives it its name. The nuts are poisonous, so admire them and leave them.

The square around it holds the Salt Lake City and County Building, finished in 1894 and Utah's first state capitol from 1896 to 1915. Nobody has written down whether the buckeye was planted before or after any of that.

The register's measurement dates from 2018, and the newest observation we can find is of its neighbour, in May 2025, not of this trunk. It was standing at the last count. If you pass the southwest corner of the square, tell us how it looks, and if you know its age, tell us that too.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the narrower of two big trees at the southwest corner of Washington Square, its crown about 14 metres across. The broad hackberry stands about 15 metres away.

trees.name: The Temple Square Wych Elm

location.address: Temple Square, northeast corner of the Tabernacle, Salt Lake City

trees.access: Free; Temple Square grounds are open to visitors daily (grounds hours set by the owner, the church)
trees.transport: Downtown; Temple Square is a short walk from the Temple Square or Gallivan Center TRAX stops
trees.story:
Utah's biggest wych elm is a European tree growing at the corner of one of the most recognisable buildings in the American West. The state's register measured it in 2019 at 25.6 metres tall, with a trunk 414 centimetres round and a crown 22.9 metres across, and ranks it first of its species in Utah. It stands at the northeast corner of the Tabernacle on Temple Square.

Wych elm is native to Europe, from the Scottish glens to the mountains of the east, and Dutch elm disease has taken enormous numbers of mature ones there. A trunk over four metres round, standing in a city block in the Great Basin, is a tree many European parks no longer have.

The building beside it was raised between 1864 and 1867, first used for the church's October 1867 conference and dedicated in 1875. No source we have found says when the elm was planted, so we cannot say how much of the Tabernacle's history it has stood beside.

The square has been under a long renovation centred on the Salt Lake Temple, expected to finish by the end of 2026. The whole west side of the square, where the Tabernacle stands, has been open to visitors again since February 2025, and an observation logged at this spot in September 2026 shows a tree standing there. Entry to the grounds is free.

Nobody has dated it. If you know, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size, 414 centimetres round and 25.6 metres tall, with a crown about 23 metres wide. It stands at the northeast corner of the Tabernacle on Temple Square.

trees.name: The Temple Square Cedar of Lebanon

location.address: Temple Square, southeast corner of the Salt Lake Temple, Salt Lake City

trees.access: Free; Temple Square grounds are open to visitors daily (grounds hours set by the owner, the church)
trees.transport: Downtown; short walk from the Temple Square or Gallivan Center TRAX stops
trees.story:
Temple Square's famous cedar is said to have arrived around 1949 in a suitcase, seven inches tall. The Deseret News told its story in 1995: the seedling came in the luggage of a Mrs. Petty of Sugar House and was planted in a corner of the square. Its top was later sheared off, and the gardeners trained a side branch up as a new leader. When the South Visitors' Center was built, the cedar was still marked for removal by oversight; a gardener, Peter Lassig, caught the mistake, and the architect, Emil Fetzer, stopped the crews.

It was nearly lost again in 2020. As the Salt Lake Temple's seismic renovation began, crews removed many trees around the 1893 temple, and the church said a tall, 70-year-old Cedar of Lebanon would be kept, with great efforts to preserve it while they excavated around it.

Utah's big tree register lists the state champion Cedar of Lebanon at the southeast corner of the temple, measured in 2019 at 20.1 metres tall, with a trunk 277 centimetres round and a crown 18.6 metres across. That is almost certainly the suitcase cedar, but no source we found names both together, so take the join as ours.

The register measured it before the excavation, and we have no dated sighting since. The renovation is expected to finish by the end of 2026 and parts of the square have been closed during the work. If you see it, tell us how it came through.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as an evergreen conifer 20 metres tall on a trunk 277 centimetres round. It stands at the southeast corner of the Salt Lake Temple.

trees.name: The Mount Olivet Cemetery Linden

location.address: Mt. Olivet Cemetery, 1342 W 500 S, Salt Lake City
location.neighbourhood: Foothill / Salt Lake City east side

trees.access: Free; Mount Olivet is a public cemetery, open in daylight
trees.transport: East bench; reached by car or bus, no walk time established
trees.story:
Utah's champion small-leaved lime has a trunk 4.11 metres round, and its crown is almost as wide as the tree is tall.

The state's big tree register, kept by the Utah Division of Forestry, Fire and State Lands, measured it in 2016: 21.0 metres tall, with a spread of 20.7 metres. In the United States this species usually goes by littleleaf linden, and this is the largest one the register knows of in the state. It stands in Mount Olivet Cemetery, and the register marks it as open to the public.

That is where the certainty ends. The register's own record disagrees with itself: its street address points to the west side of the city, while its coordinate sits on the east bench. Our pin follows the coordinate and is approximate, and in a cemetery this size that leaves you looking among a great many trees. The register's measurements are the best guide: a lime this broad, with a trunk over four metres round, should not be easy to confuse with its neighbours.

The 2016 measurement is also the last sighting we have, so we cannot promise the tree is still standing. Nobody has dated it. If you find it, tell us where exactly it stands and how it looks, and if you know when it was planted, tell us that too. Come in July, when this species carries its small, scented flowers, later than most limes.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size: a trunk 4.11 metres round and a crown about 20 metres across, the state champion of its species. It stands somewhere in Mount Olivet Cemetery; our pin is approximate.

best_time.label: July, when the small-leaved lime flowers and its scent carries

trees.name: The Peace Gardens Bur Oak

location.address: International Peace Gardens, Jordan Park, 1060 S 900 W, Salt Lake City (north-east corner of the gardens)

Owner of the ground: Salt Lake City. Both PUBLIC_ACCESS = Yes. Register-only, one source (US: one credible source is enough), flagged. Alive: both measured 2026; lifecheck RECENT only for the park generally (an iNaturalist hibiscus 2026-09-20 within 60 m), no observation of the oaks themselves. Pin is register-grade, not placed on a crown: approximate; the gardens are a walk-through garden so no location_site. trees.story:
Two of Utah's champion oaks stand about 15 metres apart in one corner of the International Peace Gardens. The state's big tree register places both in the north-east corner of the gardens in Jordan Park, and both were measured in 2026.

This entry is the bur oak, the largest of its species the register knows of in Utah. Its trunk is 330 centimetres round and it stands 22.6 metres tall, but the figure that tells you what it looks like is the spread. The crown reaches about 26 metres across, wider than the tree is high, the shape of an oak that has had open ground on every side.

Its neighbour is a northern red oak, champion of its own species, 305 centimetres round and 25.3 metres tall. So the slimmer of the pair is the taller one, and its crown is only a couple of metres narrower. Two record oaks of two species, close enough to take in from one spot on the path.

Bur oak is a tree of the American Midwest and the prairie edge, known for big acorns sitting in fringed, mossy-looking cups. Here it grows in a free city garden open from seven in the morning until eleven at night, with flower displays around it from May to October.

Jordan Park dates from 1918, but no source says when either oak was planted, and the register gives no age for them. If you know when they went in, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, about 26 metres across and wider than the tree is tall. It stands in the north-east corner of the Peace Gardens, some 15 metres from the taller, slimmer champion red oak.

trees.name: The University of Utah Japanese Zelkova

location.address: University of Utah campus, grass area west/north-west of the William Stewart Building (Bld 6), Salt Lake City

official_register.name: Utah Big Tree Register (Division of Forestry, Fire and State Lands ArcGIS layer, objectid 323)

trees.access: Free, open campus lawn; the University of Utah campus is a designated state arboretum with a self-guided tree tour (QR placards, no ticket).
trees.transport: University of Utah campus, about 4 km east of Temple Square; TRAX University line serves the campus (stop and walk time not verified).
trees.verify_notes: Register row objectid 323 (owner University of Utah, PUBLIC_ACCESS = Yes): circumference 153 in = 389 cm, height 63 ft = 19.2 m, spread 97 ft = 29.6 m, measured 2026, new entry updated 2026-07, state champion status 1. Second source and ground owner: University of Utah Facilities tree tour page for Japanese Zelkova (page last updated 7/29/26) says large specimens stand in the grass area west of the William Stewart Building (Bld 6) or along the south side of Student Services Building (Bld 40), and that the tree west of the Stewart Building is on the Utah Big Tree Registry. So species, location area and register listing are two-source confirmed. Register coordinate (40.76345,-111.851186) is IDENTICAL to the Lacebark Elm row objectid 325 ('west of Crocker Science Center'), so it is a shared campus point, not a trunk fix: precision approximate, a campus is not a small site. Press search summary (not fetched, unverified) said a university piece calls it the largest of its kind in Utah and planted by botanist Walter Cottam; do not use without fetching attheu.utah.edu. Alive: measured 2026-07 area; lifecheck NONE at the pin, nothing independent. No age in sources; none invented. Cluster: the lead file also lists the Chinese Cork Oak, Mongolian Oak, Lacebark Elm, German Ash, and Port Orford Cedar register rows on the same campus within ~500 m, a walkable champion walk.
trees.story:
This zelkova is ten metres wider than it is tall. Utah's big tree register measured it in 2026 at 19.2 metres high, on a trunk 389 centimetres round, with a crown spreading 29.6 metres, and lists it as the state champion of its species.

That breadth is the species doing what it does when nothing is in the way. A zelkova typically sends many upright limbs out from a short trunk, fanning like the ribs of a vase, and on an open lawn they keep going. Saw-leaf zelkova comes from Japan, Korea and China. In America it was promoted as a street tree to stand in for the elms that disease killed, so most you meet are young and narrow. This one has had room.

It grows on the University of Utah campus, which is a designated state arboretum. The university's own self-guided tree tour sends you to the grass west of the William Stewart Building and says the tree there is on the state register. QR placards on the tour stand in for a guide, and there is no ticket.

The register lists several other state champions within a few hundred metres on the same campus, among them a Chinese cork oak, a Mongolian oak and a lacebark elm, so the zelkova can be the first stop of a short walk rather than the only one.

No source gives a planting date. If you know when it went in, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, almost 30 metres across, far wider than the tree is tall. It stands on the grass west of the William Stewart Building, the spot the campus tree tour names.

trees.name: The Murray City Arboretum Baldcypress

location.address: Murray City Park arboretum, 296 E Murray Park Ave, Murray

official_register.name: Utah Big Tree Register (Utah Community Forest Council directory, objectid 121)

trees.transport: Murray City Park, about 15 km south of downtown Salt Lake City by TRAX (Murray Central, roughly 1.5 km from the park, estimated, not verified).
trees.verify_notes: Register row objectid 121 (owner Murray City, PUBLIC_ACCESS = Yes): circumference 121 in = 307 cm, height 67 ft = 20.4 m, spread 50 ft, measured 2026, entry updated 2026-06, nominated 2015, state champion 1, not national. Register-only; Wikipedia confirms the park has an arboretum but nothing names this tree. Flagged: register only, one source. Alive: measured 2026; lifecheck RECENT 2026-07-04 only for the area (an iNaturalist observation near the pin). Pin register-grade, park arboretum is not a small site: approximate. Baldcypress is an eastern US swamp species planted in a Utah arboretum, which is the interest. No age; none invented. Murray arboretum established Arbor Day 1961 per an ActiveRain blog (not a source), do not use. Same arboretum holds register rows for Flowering Pear, Halfelm, Black Alder, Brewer Spruce, Chinese Fringetree within ~100 m (existing open leads). Borderline worth-the-walk: the smallest girth of the three, only ship if the writer needs a Murray point.
trees.story:
Utah's biggest bald cypress is a swamp tree living in one of the driest states in the country. The species belongs to the wetlands of the American Southeast, the river bottoms and bayous where it grows with its feet in standing water. This one grows in the arboretum of Murray City Park, south of Salt Lake City, on ordinary park ground.

It seems not to mind. The state's big tree register, which first listed it in 2015, measured it in 2026 at 20.4 metres tall, on a trunk 307 centimetres round, with a crown about 15 metres across, and ranks it the champion of its species in Utah. That is a modest tree by the standards of a Louisiana bayou and a remarkable one for a city park at the foot of the Wasatch.

The other thing it does is less expected of a conifer. A bald cypress is deciduous. In autumn its soft needles turn copper red and then the whole tree drops them, so through the winter it stands bare, which is where the name comes from.

The arboretum holds several other trees on the same state register within about a hundred metres, among them a Chinese fringetree, a Brewer spruce and a black alder, so a slow lap of it takes in more than one champion. The park is owned by the city and free to enter.

Nobody has recorded when the cypress was planted, and the register gives no age. If you know, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it in autumn, when its needles turn copper red and fall, which no spruce or pine does. It stands in the arboretum of Murray City Park, about 20 metres tall on a trunk 307 centimetres round.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the needles turn copper red before the whole tree drops them

trees.story:
The university's own tree tour calls this oak a unique specimen, and the state agrees it is the biggest of its kind in Utah. The Utah Big Tree Register measured it in 2026 at 19.8 metres tall, on a trunk 196 centimetres round, with a crown about 18 metres across, and lists it as the state champion.

The species is an East Asian oak, and the thing to look at is the bark. It grows thick, ridged and corky, soft enough in look to explain the name, although the cork of wine bottles comes from a different oak in the western Mediterranean. Seeing one this size in a high, dry desert valley is the surprise. Salt Lake City is not where anyone would expect an oak from China, Korea and Japan to reach state-record size.

It stands on the University of Utah campus, south of the John R. Park Building. Within about 40 metres stand two more state champions, a German ash and a Mongolian oak, so the lawn south of the Park Building holds three record trees in a few steps. A saw-leaf zelkova and a lacebark elm, champions too, stand about 110 metres to the south-west.

Our pin is the register's point near the spot, not a fix on the trunk, so read the bark to be sure. Nobody has published when it was planted. If you know, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the bark, thick, ridged and corky, on a trunk about 2 metres round. It stands south of the John R. Park Building, within 40 metres of the champion German ash and Mongolian oak.

trees.story:
The University of Utah has exactly one of these ashes, and it is the biggest in the state. The campus tree tour calls it rare and the only specimen, and the Utah Big Tree Register lists it as state champion, measured in 2026 at 16.5 metres tall on a trunk 254 centimetres round, with a crown nearly 17 metres across.

The name needs a footnote. The register and the tour both call it German ash, but Fraxinus holotricha is a tree of south-east Europe, as the tour itself says, and most references call it Balkan ash or hairy ash. We use the register's label so the two match, and the Latin name settles which tree is meant.

What makes the stop worth it is the company. The ash stands on the lawn south of the John R. Park Building, and within about 40 metres grow two more state champions, an Oriental cork oak with thick corky bark and a Mongolian oak. Three record trees from three corners of Eurasia, on one patch of grass in a desert city, a few steps apart. A champion saw-leaf zelkova and a lacebark elm stand about 110 metres to the south-west if you want to keep walking.

The grounds are open and there is no ticket. Our pin is the register's point near the spot rather than a fix on the trunk. Nobody has recorded when it was planted. If you know, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the stoutest of the three champions south of the John R. Park Building, its trunk 254 centimetres round. The corky-barked cork oak and the slimmer Mongolian oak stand within 40 metres.

trees.story:
This is the smallest of the champions on the University of Utah lawn, and it still holds a state record. The Utah Big Tree Register measured it in 2026 at 13.1 metres tall, on a trunk 152 centimetres round, with a crown exactly as wide as the tree is high, and lists it as the largest Mongolian oak in Utah. The campus tree tour calls it rare and the only specimen on the grounds.

The size is the story in reverse. Mongolian oak is a tree of north-east Asia, from Siberia's far east through northern China, Korea and Japan, and the tour describes it as slow growing. A trunk that reads as ordinary next to a city park oak is, for this species in this place, as big as anyone has found.

On its own it would not justify the trip. As part of a group it does. It stands south of the John R. Park Building, and within about 40 metres grow two more state champions, an Oriental cork oak with thick, corky bark and the campus's single German ash. A champion zelkova and lacebark elm stand about 110 metres to the south-west. Five records in a ten-minute walk, all on open grounds with no ticket.

Our pin is the register's point near the spot, not a fix on the trunk. Nobody has published when it was planted. If you know, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the smallest of the three champions south of the John R. Park Building, its trunk 152 centimetres round and its crown about 13 metres across, as wide as it is tall.

trees.story:
Lacebark elms usually stop at 12 to 15 metres. This one, by the state's measure, is 23.2. The Utah Big Tree Register recorded it in 2026 at that height, on a trunk 259 centimetres round, with a crown about 18 metres across, and lists it as the state champion of its species. The University of Utah's own tree tour gives 40 to 50 feet as typical, so the register's figure is half again as tall as the species is supposed to grow.

The bark is the reason to look closely. It flakes away in patches, leaving a mottled trunk of grey-green, orange and brown, which is where the name comes from. The tree is native to China, Korea and Japan, and is often sold as Chinese elm.

Where exactly it stands needs a caveat. The register places it west of the Crocker Science Center; the campus tour says west of the George Thomas Building. The register's coordinate is also identical to the one it gives for the champion saw-leaf zelkova, so it is a shared campus point rather than a fix on either trunk. Both sources agree on the area, and the two big trees may stand within metres of each other. The mottled bark is how you tell them apart.

Three more champions, a cork oak, a German ash and a Mongolian oak, grow about 110 metres to the north-east, south of the Park Building. Nobody has dated this elm. If you know when it went in, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the bark, flaking in mottled patches of grey-green, orange and brown. It stands west of the George Thomas Building, the spot the campus tree tour gives; the register says west of the Crocker Science Center.

trees.story:
A tree from the fog belt of the Pacific coast has grown into a state record in the Utah desert. Port Orford cedar is native to a narrow strip of south-west Oregon and north-west California, where sea mist keeps it wet most of the year. The Utah Big Tree Register lists this one on the University of Utah campus as the largest in the state, at 22.6 metres tall on a trunk 239 centimetres round, with a crown about 15.5 metres across.

Those numbers are from 2018. The register has not remeasured it since, unlike the other campus champions it updated in 2026, so the figures are eight years old.

The sources also differ in what they know. The campus tree tour lists the species under its other name, Lawson falsecypress, calls it uncommon and sends you west of the George Thomas Building, but it does not mention the state register for this tree. The register is the one source for the record. Despite the name it is not a true cedar but a cypress relative, with flat sprays of scale leaves.

In winter it earns the detour twice over. The campus champions around it, the zelkova, the lacebark elm, the oaks and the ash by the Park Building, are all deciduous, and this is the one still green when the rest are bare.

Nobody has recorded when it was planted. If you know, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the evergreen among the campus champions, a conifer about 22 metres tall with flat sprays of scale leaves. It stands west of the George Thomas Building, the spot the campus tree tour gives.
